entities.summary:
Xenophon of Ephesus was a Greek novelist from the Roman Imperial period, likely active in the 2nd or 3rd century CE, whose singular surviving work, the *Ephesian Tale of Anthia and Habrocomes* (often called *Ephesiaka*), stands as a pivotal text in the development of the ancient Greek novel. While details of his life remain elusive, his contribution to the nascent genre of prose fiction significantly shaped narrative traditions, offering a foundational model for tales of star-crossed lovers and perilous adventures that would resonate for centuries. His work provides invaluable insight into the literary tastes and cultural anxieties of the Roman East, bridging the classical Greek literary heritage with emerging forms of popular entertainment.

The *Ephesiaka* recounts the epic journey of the beautiful Anthia and Habrocomes, a young couple from Ephesus, who fall deeply in love, are separated by pirates and fate, endure numerous trials including slavery, false deaths, and forced marriages, only to be reunited through divine intervention and their unwavering fidelity. Divided into five books, the narrative features exotic locales across the Mediterranean world, from Egypt to Italy, and incorporates elements of romance, adventure, melodrama, and religious devotion, particularly to the goddess Artemis. This complex plot structure, involving mistaken identities, dramatic reversals, and miraculous rescues, showcases a sophisticated understanding of storytelling techniques that captivated ancient audiences.
